It is a process of asexual reproduction in which the nucleus divides multiple times, and the cytoplasm divides later to form daughter cells.
Many offsprings are produced. E.g. Plasmodium (malarial parasite ).

3. Fragmentation
It is a process of asexual reproduction in which the body breaks into pieces, and each fragment grows into a new organism.
It occurs in simple multicellular organisms. E.g. Spirogyra (green algae), Rhodophyte (red algae), and sea anemone.
Breaks into half which is not fully developed but later develops into a complete spirogyra Fragment § Fragmentation in Spirogyra 4. Budding
It is a process of asexual reproduction in which a new organism develops from a bud or outgrowth on the parent organism.
A small bud forms on the parent body due to cell division.
It grows and detaches to form a new organism.
Itoccurs in simple multicellular and unicellular organisms.
E.g. Hydra (multicellular) and Yeast (unicellular).

6. Vegetative Propagation

It is a process of asexual reproduction in which a new plant grows from the vegetative parts of the parent plant, such as the root, stem, or leaf. It can also occur through cutting or grafting parts of the plant.
This method does not involve seeds, and the new plant is genetically identical to the parent.

8. Spore Formation
It is a process of asexual reproduction in which an organism produces spores — tiny, usually single-celled structures, that can grow into new individuals under favorable conditions.
E.g. Spore formation in Rhizopus (bread mould) a type of fungi.

Sexual reproduction in plants involves the fusion of male and female gametes (pollen and ovule) to form a zygote, which develops into a seed that grows into a new plant.
This process occurs through flowers, the reproductive organs of plants.
In syncarpous conditions, more than one pistil fuse together.
Androecium- All male parts of plants.
Gynoecium - All female parts of plants.
Chlamydomonas is considered unicellular green algae.
1. Bisexual Flowers (Hermaphrodite Flowers)
These flowers contain both male (stamens) and female (pistil) reproductive organs in the same flower.
They are capable of self-pollination as well as cross- pollination.
E.g. Hibiscus, mustard, lily, sunflower.
2. Unisexual Flowers
These flowers contain only one reproductive organ + either stamens or pistil, but not both.
They are capable of cross-pollination. E.g. Male flower that has only stamens — Corn, Cucumber, Female flower that only has carpels + Papaya, watermelon.
Monoecious Plants: Male and female reproductive parts are present on the same plant. E.g. Maize, cucumber.
Dioecious Plants: Male and female reproductive parts are present on separate plants.
E.g. Papaya, date palm.
Anatomy of a Flower
Male reproductive part (collectively called Stamen) consists of:
Filament: Supports anther.
~ Anther: Produces pollen (yellow colour).
Female reproductive part (collectively called Pistil) consists of:
Stigma: Sticky bulb that catches pollen.
Style: Passageway for pollen.
Ovary: The part of pistil that holds the eggs awaiting fertilization and later becomes the fruit.
Isogamy: Fusion of morphologically similar gametes (same size and shape). E.g. Chlamydomonas.
Anisogamy: Fusion of morphologically dissimilar gametes (different size and shape). E.g. Some algae, fungi.
Oogamy: A type of anisogamy where large, non-motile egg fuses with small, motile sperm. E.g. humans Pollination

Pollination is the process where pollen, containing a plant's male reproductive cells, is transferred to the female part of a plant (stigma). This transfer is essential for plant reproduction, leading to fertilization and the development of seeds.
T Pollination:
Pollen from anther is transferred to the stigma of the same flower or another flower on the same plant.
No genetic variation. E.g. Pea, tomato.
Pollen is transferred from the anther of one flower to the stigma of another flower on a different plant of the same species.
Promotes genetic diversity. E.g. Apple, sunflower.

After pollination, the pollen grain germinates on the stigma and forms a pollen tube that carries the male gamete to the ovule in the ovary.
Male and female gametes fuse to form the Zygote. Zygote develops into an embryo. The ovule becomes seed and ovary becomes fruit.
A fruit that develops from other parts of a flower, in addition to ovary, and does not require fertilisation. In this type of fertilization, thallus is also involved. E.g. Apple, cashew nut.

It is a type of fruit with a hard shell that includes a seed and has an inner flesh. E.g. Coconut.

Ovaries produce eggs (ova) and estrogen + progesterone (female sex hormones).
A female is born with all the egg cells (oocytes) she will ever have. At the age of 12, the ovaries start to mature.
2. Fallopian Tubes (Oviducts)
The site where sperm meet egg and fertilization occurs.
The cilia inside the fallopian tubes push the egg towards the uterus.

3. Uterus (Womb)
Muscular organ where a fertilized egg implants and develops into a foetus. The innermost lining of the uterus is called endometrium.
The cervix is the lower part of the uterus that connects to the vagina. During childbirth, it must open to allow the baby to pass through.

Thickening of uterine wall for preparation for potential implantation of fertilised egg during pregnancy. When pregnancy does not occur after the uterine lining thickens, the lining is shed through menstruation.

Menopause is the permanent cessation of menstruation in women, marking the end of their reproductive years.

It typically occurs in the late 40s to early 50s, with the average age being around 51. This stage is characterized by the ovaries no longer releasing eggs and a decrease in the production of estrogen and progesterone.
Fertilization is the process where a male gamete (sperm) and a female gamete (egg) fuse to form a zygote, which is the first cell of a new individual.
Types of Fertilisation:
1. Internal Fertilisation: The process of a sperm cell and an egg cell fusing inside the female body during reproduction. E.g. in humans.
2. External Fertilisation: A reproductive process where a male sperm fertilises a female's egg outside of the female's body. E.g. Frog, earthworms, crab.
Viviparous: Animals that develop inside the parent's body and give birth to live offspring. E.g. Cats, dogs, humans.
Ovoviviparous: Animals that lay eggs and the eggs develop inside mother's body. E.g. Sharks, snakes, some fishes (like guppies).
Oviparous: Animals that lay eggs and the eggs develop outside the mother's body. E.g. Birds, frogs, lizards, (Exception: Platypus is the only mammal reproduced oviparously).
Process of Fertilization Pri involv
1. Gametogenesis: This is the process of forming gametes — Sperm in males and eggs in females, essential for reproduction.
2. Insemination: It involves the transfer of sperm into the female reproductive tract during intercourse. MElamOrphOSis uD UNELLY)
3. Fertilisation: The sperm meets and fuses with the egg, forming a zygote (the first cell of the new baby).
4. Implantation: The zygote develops into a blastocyst and attaches itself to the uterine wall, beginning pregnancy.
5. Gestation: This is the period of development where the embryo grows and forms into a foetus inside the uterus.
6. Parturition: The final stage, where the baby is delivered through childbirth.
